facts.fact: Vietnamese name for the term: "Chu trình nitơ".
English name for the term: "Nitrogen Cycle".
Variant Vietnamese spelling for the term: "Chu trình Nito".
Vietnamese keepers' slang for the process: "Cycle nước".
Alternative Vietnamese name for the term: "chu kỳ Nitơ".
Short name for the process used by a Vietnamese shop: "Cycle".
Vietnamese spelling for the term: "chu trình Ni-tơ".
Alternative Vietnamese name for the term: "vòng tuần hoàn nitơ".
Fish excrete ammonia across their gills into the water. Biofilter bacteria convert it to nitrite and then to nitrate through aerobic processes.
Nitrosomonas bacteria (aerobic) convert ammonia/ammonium to nitrite, and Nitrobacter bacteria (aerobic) convert nitrite to nitrate.
One Vietnamese shop names Nitrospira, not Nitrobacter, as the bacteria that convert nitrite to nitrate.
Anaerobic denitrifying bacteria turn nitrate into nitrogen gas. They form in live rock and in substrate deeper than about 5 cm.
Waste, leftover food and decaying organic matter release ammonia (NH3) and ammonium (NH4+).
Most test kits measure total ammonia nitrogen (TAN), which includes both toxic un-ionized ammonia (NH3) and less toxic ammonium (NH4+).
Freshwater fish usually tolerate TAN below 1 mg/L. Un-ionized ammonia below 0.05 mg/L is not considered harmful, though tolerance varies by species.
The share of TAN present as toxic NH3 rises as pH and temperature rise. pH has more influence than temperature.
Above pH 7 more of the ammonia stays as toxic NH3, and below pH 7 more of it is NH4+.
Nitrite toxicity is listed at NO2 above 0.1 mg/L, with tremendous species-specific variation.
Most kits report nitrite as nitrite-nitrogen. Multiply the reading by 3.3 to get NO2.
Nitrate is less toxic than ammonia or nitrite. The recommended level for freshwater is below 20 mg/L.
Most kits report nitrate as nitrate-nitrogen. Multiply the reading by 4.4 to get NO3. Nitrate toxicity is listed at NO3-N of 70 mg/L or more.
One Vietnamese shop gives targets of ammonia near 0 ppm, nitrite 0 ppm and nitrate 15–50 ppm. It says nitrate below 15 ppm is poor for planted freshwater tanks.
One Vietnamese shop says nitrate becomes toxic above 20 ppm.
Plants can use nitrate as a nutrient. Nitrate is also removed by water changes and anaerobic bacteria.
Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter both work best at 25–30°C.
Nitrosomonas works from pH 6.0 to 9.0, best at about 7.8–8.0. Nitrobacter works best at pH 7.3–7.5.
Dissolved oxygen should be above 6 mg/L. The cycle stops if oxygen falls below 2 mg/L.
New tank syndrome: ammonia and/or nitrite rise during the first 2–3 weeks because the biofilter bacteria have not developed yet.
Signs of ammonia toxicity (new tank syndrome) are lethargy, anorexia, spinning, convulsive swimming and darkened colour.
Signs of nitrite toxicity are piping at the surface, and gills and blood turning dark brown, though the colour can be hard to see.
Nitrite can cause brown blood disease. Affected fish gather near the surface or pipe for oxygen.
Chronic nitrate exposure can cause lethargy and swelling around the throat (thyroid hyperplasia, 'goiter').
The biofilter has matured when TAN and nitrite peak and fall, followed by a rise in nitrate.
The cycle is complete when NH3/NH4 and NO2 readings on API or JBL test kits drop to or near 0.

Timeline of a cycle: the ammonia stage lasts 7 to 10 days, and Nitrosomonas appears around day 10. Nitrite peaks around 15 ppm and falls below 2–3 ppm by about day 30. Nitrobacter takes over around day 20.
Overfeeding and failure of the biofilter are common causes of high ammonia.
Low chloride in freshwater is a risk factor for nitrite toxicity. pH above 8 is listed alongside the ammonia toxicity threshold.
Dechlorinating chloramine with sodium thiosulfate releases ammonia. Repeated water changes can then build up toxic ammonia, especially in new or damaged biofilters.
Do a water change of at least 50% as soon as high ammonia is detected.
Reduce or stop feeding until the ammonia problem is corrected.
If TAN is above 5 mg/L and pH is below 7, move the fish to a clean, tempered system. Otherwise the ammonia shifts quickly to toxic NH3 as the pH rises.
Check whether the source water contains ammonia or chloramine, since water changes can add ammonia.
When ammonia or nitrite is high, change 30–50% of the water daily until levels drop to about 2 ppm or 0 ppm.
Chloride competitively blocks nitrite uptake at the gills. Many aquaria and ponds keep a residual salinity of 1–3 ppt, which makes nitrite toxicity less likely.
Salt may be used to halt deaths during a sudden nitrite spike in many freshwater fish, together with a water change and filter maintenance. The Merck manual gives no exact emergency dose.
Prime or Amquel can help during an ammonia spike, but they convert ammonia to a less toxic form rather than remove it.
Use a dechlorinator designed for chloramines that also binds the released ammonia.
A new biofilter usually takes about 6 weeks to become fully established.
A full cycle takes 2 to 24 weeks depending on conditions. With good bacterial supplements added regularly, it can be cut to about 2 weeks.
Monitor TAN and nitrite daily and do frequent water changes until the biofilter has cycled.
"Feed" the biofilter with fish food or ammonium chloride before adding fish, and use commercial nitrifying bacteria from a reputable source.

Steps: set up the tank and run the filter. Aerate, because the bacteria use a lot of oxygen. Optionally add Seachem Stability or media, water or filter floss from an established tank. Then wait before adding livestock.
After adding Seachem Stability, wait about 4 to 5 days before adding fish and 2 to 3 weeks before adding shrimp.
Seachem Stability dose for a new tank: on day 1, add 1 capful (5 mL) for each 40 L (10 US gallons) with UV/ozone turned off. On days 2–7, add 1 capful (5 mL) for every 80 L (20 US gallons) daily.
Seachem says fish can be added at any time if Stability dosing continues for the full 7 days, and that it is harmless to all aquatic organisms and plants.
Used water or filter media from another tank can shorten the cycle to about 3 to 7 days, sometimes as little as 2 days. Cycling with a few fish often takes several weeks.
Freshwater upkeep: change about 30% of the water weekly. Around day 27, when nitrate starts rising, change about 40%.
Keep the filter running so it stays a home for the beneficial bacteria, and add filter media only from an established tank whose fish are all healthy.
Add fish slowly to a new system. Avoid overfeeding, overstocking, and antimicrobials or chemicals that damage the biofilter.
Run the filter 24/7, and replace only part of the water at a time.
Replace filter media gradually: put new media in the tank 7–10 days before removing the old.
In freshwater tanks, add aquatic plants to absorb nitrate.
Rinsing filter media under tap water kills the beneficial bacteria, because tap water can contain chlorine.
Switching the filter on and off often, or replacing all the water at once, disrupts the bacteria.
Adding fish or plants before the cycle is stable can lead to root rot and fish deaths.
Adding fish during the ammonia stage is a mistake, because they are very prone to disease then.
Skipping aeration during the cycle is a mistake, because the cycle uses a lot of oxygen.
Seachem Stability does not remove chlorine from tap water, so tap water still needs dechlorinating.
Ignoring nitrite is a mistake: it is toxic even at low levels.
Chlorine in household tap water ("nước máy sinh hoạt") can harm plants, fish, shrimp and other tank life.
Ways to dechlorinate tap water: store it in a container for 3 to 4 days, aerate it in a container for 24 hours, or add Seachem Prime.
One Vietnamese shop sells Extra Bio bacteria ("Men Vi Sinh Extra Bio Cao Cấp") for starting the cycle. It gives no dose.
During the cycle, keep the tank out of direct sunlight, and turn the lights off only for the cycle, not permanently.
A Vietnamese shop says the cycle usually finishes 1 to 2 weeks after setup. The Merck manual instead says a new biofilter usually takes about 6 weeks to become fully established.
